concepts.concept_description: Using the 'forever' block to create a sequence of actions that repeats endlessly. In the example, a sprite moves continuously across the screen.
Using the 'repeat' block to execute a set of commands a specific number of times, as opposed to a 'forever' loop which runs infinitely.
Using the 'when green flag clicked' block to start a script when the project is initiated.
Using the 'if on edge, bounce' block within a loop to make a sprite reverse direction upon reaching the edge of the stage.
Using the 'move steps' block to change a sprite's position along its current direction.
Using the 'set rotation style' block to control how a sprite visually orients itself, specifically to prevent it from turning upside down after bouncing off an edge.
Creating a new variable (e.g., 'emotion') and giving it an initial value using the 'set variable to' block.
Updating the value of a variable during the program to track a changing state, such as a sprite's emotion.
Using 'broadcast' and 'when I receive' blocks to enable communication and trigger scripts between different sprites.
Using the 'when this sprite clicked' event block to trigger a script when the user clicks on a specific sprite.
Using the 'join' operator to combine strings of text with the value of a variable to create dynamic messages.
Using the 'show' and 'hide' blocks to control which sprite is visible on the stage at different points in the program.
Broadcasting a message that is dynamically created by joining text with a variable, allowing for more flexible inter-sprite communication.
Making sprites display messages on the screen for a set duration using the 'say for seconds' or 'think for seconds' blocks.
The computational thinking concept of breaking down a complex problem into smaller, more manageable parts, demonstrated by coding the behavior for each emotional state of the sprite separately.
